newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgarian president urges quick election.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgarian president urges quick election.

text.p: Bulgaria's new president Petar Stoyanov was sworn in on Sunday and gave his support to opposition demands for a quick general election to end the country's political crisis.
"Bulgaria wants elections as soon as possible, Bulgaria must get these elections," Stoyanov told parliament.

The governing Socialists have offered elections by the end of the year and a second Socialist cabinet in the meantime. The opposition wants elections sooner and opposes any new government led by the former communists.
It has staged 13 consecutive days of mass protests against economic hardship blamed on the current parliamentary majority.
Socialist deputies reaffirmed their willingness to talk to the opposition but the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) signalled it would only talk to Stoyanov.

"Appointing an interim government and negotiating dissolution of parliament is entirely within the powers of the president. The UDF will hold consultations with him on this subject and we trust him to hold consultations with other political forces," said UDF spokeswoman Nadezhda Mihailova.

Stoyanov has said he may give the Socialists the mandate denied them by outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev, who said on Friday that asking them to form a new government in the current climate would only cause more trouble.
Zhelev told Bulgarian television: "There is no sense in handing a formal mandate which will explode social peace."
Stoyanov, meeting parliamentary leaders after his inauguration, said a new government needed the support of all sides in order to implement painful but vital reforms.
"Only a government based on broad national support can carry out vital economic reforms needed to haul Bulgaria out of the crisis," he told reporters.
Stoyanov and his vice president, Todor Kavaldzhiev, were sworn in by parliamentary speaker Blagovest Sendov.
Parliament was cordoned off by police but small crowds gathered behind the barricades as bells rang out from the adjacent Alexander Nevsky cathedral.
The ceremony was broadcast on national television and freezing temperatures kept many people at home.
Protesters besieged and ransacked parliament last weekend in clashes with riot police in which 196 people were injured.

"We have to make the right choice, which is the European type of civilisation, to show our will and to build the conditions for our integration into the European Union and NATO," Stoyanov said in his inaugural speech.
The government has dragged its feet on European and NATO integration, anxious not to alienate its old allies in Moscow.
"The Bulgaria of the future should resemble the countries to which our children emigrate," Stoyanov said.
"We must offer our children the society in which they dream of living, here in Bulgaria." Many young well-educated Bulgarians leave to seek a better life in wealthier countries.
The government of former communists, mired in a deep economic crisis blamed on corruption and resistance to reform, scored just eight percent support in an opinion poll last week.
Socialist reformers said a quick election could solve the crisis, but hardliners were more cautious.

Party leader Georgi Parvanov said Stoyanov's call was "not sufficiently well argued" while reformist Filip Bokov told Reuters: "It is quite realistic to hold elections at the end of March if negotiated."
UDF leader Ivan Kostov was jubilant. "This is a celebration for Bulgaria. Elections now!" he said.
The UDF invited supporters to a celebration concert near the parliament at four p.m. (1400 GMT) instead of its usual anti-government rally.

Leftist dissidents on Saturday founded a rival coalition to the Socialists, fuelling speculation that the party could lose its parliamentary majority, won in 1994 elections, even if granted a new mandate by Stoyanov.
